utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's start with the usual routine. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And General Talic, I put the same question to you. Do you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can understand you and I hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, too. So appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner and Nicholas Koumjian for the Prosecution, assisted by Ruth Karper. Your Honour, may I say that Mr. Cayley and I, as it were, are taking turns in being in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that. Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm John Ackerman. I appear with Milka Maglov, my co-counsel, and Tania Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For General Talic? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm Xavier de Roux for General Talic, and I'm assisted by Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic and Fabien Masson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, having cleared that stage, important stage, in the proceedings, we can now proceed with the continuation of the cross-examination of Witness Krzic by Maitre de Roux, but I see -- I recognise Mr. Ackerman on his feet. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This morning, I provided the Chamber with the rest of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen it. It's not conclusive, and in any case, let's be practical about it, Mr. Ackerman. Maitre de Roux needs a whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please do not hear me as asking for that day. I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will go today and change my reservations and change my plans regarding Sarajevo because yesterday I told you I would, and that's what I'll do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's very much appreciated, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The other thing that I wanted to do, before I forget to do it today, is request permission of the Tribunal for my co-counsel Ms. Maglov to be absent from our hearings next week. She will return a week from Monday. She has obligations with regard to this case in Banja Luka that I've asked her to perform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Permission granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you please bring in the witness, Mr. Muharem Krzic? Ms. Korner, incidentally, just to -- I would imagine that you've been updated by Mr. Cayley and Mr. Koumjian, but we have had in the course of the last two days, a number of documents that were shown to the witness and supposedly they will be exhibited at the end of his evidence. Just to remind you that this still has to be done. That's number 1. And that if there are any other documents related to his evidence that you may not have brought forward, that you make them available. I don't know if there are any but I have a suspicion that there might be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I'm aware, all the exhibits that we intend to -- that we intend to put through this witness have been produced already. But I'm certainly aware of the fact that they've still got to be given numbers, and if there are any others --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They were given temporary numbers at the same time, simultaneously, as they were being brought forward, which I suppose will be the number that we would best follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that was the whole idea behind the exercise that we went through last week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If I may, we will confirm those numbers at the end of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please. It's very important so that -- because what I am doing, at least from this side, is that I have compiled, and later on I will have in the same folder, witnesses' testimony, the entire testimony, including that of cross-examination and all the documentation that -- to which he has referred or asked -- has been asked to make reference to. So it is important that we stick to the same numbering because it will be very important for future reference, okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we quite understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, bring him in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krzic. You will now be handed the same document on which there is a solemn declaration which you are kindly asked to read out and make. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down. And now, Mr. de Roux has -- Mr. de Roux, Xavier de Roux, counsel for General Talic, will continue his cross-examination and will be directing some questions to you. Yes, Mr. de Roux.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krzic, while I was rereading your book, your testimony, I noticed that you always called the Serbs "Chetniks." Isn't that a derogative term, and why do you always use this term?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry that you got this impression. I have to deny that. I didn't always use members or some of the members of the Serbian people. I didn't always call them Chetniks. But that term has been present in our territory for over a century, has been familiar, and it always related to people who carried weapons. As far as the Bosniaks are concerned, we always had terrible experiences with people for whom this synonym, this term, was used. This term remind us Bosniaks of the genocide that was committed in our territory, and not for the first time. Personally, I think -- when I use the term "Chetnik," I am thinking of people who hate other peoples and who, because of their hatred, are prepared to use the most ruthless means. This term is historically very clear. It has been clarified. I don't see why I should clarify it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's return to 1992 -- 1990, when the Congress of the League of Communists failed. There were elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The three nationalist parties that were present, neither of them won a majority vote. And an agreement was signed between these three parties: the SDA, your party; the SDS; and the HDZ. What was the objective of this agreement, and what were the rules?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have that -- I haven't had that agreement in my hands and I haven't seen it in its entirety, if we're talking about an agreement at the level of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I haven't even seen the written part at the level of the municipality of Banja Luka, from the municipality of Banja Luka. But the agreement between those three, let's say nationalist parties, at that time was made - and this is something I'm deeply convinced of - firstly, because in the course of the elections themselves, there was much fear that the left parties, that is to say the Communist Parties, would win the majority and that Bosnia-Herzegovina would remain under the influence of the Communist Party. So each party, as far as I know, saw a particular danger for itself, saw the danger of each party fighting for its own people, its own nation. As the Bosniaks are concerned -- as far as the Bosniaks is concerned, we thought that if the Communist Parties continued to govern, that would prolong -- that would extend all the negative elements that were present during the communist regime. I won't go into them all. We were ready, therefore, to cooperate with parties who had at least stated that they were democratic but that weren't prepared to support, let's say, the Communist Parties. According to that agreement, there's only one thing that I am aware of: A division of government, a sharing of government was agreed on in accordance with that agreement, which would be proportional, which would represent the election results of each party, whereas the votes of the left parties would also be distributed proportionally. I will give you an example. If the left party got 100 votes, then -- in the case of Banja Luka, 48 plus the remaining part that is to be divided out of those 100 votes would be votes for the SDS. In the case of the SDA, that would be 13, plus the remainder of the votes, et cetera, et cetera. So that was an agreement, as far as I know, in which no essential agreements had been reached on the strategic future, first of all, of Yugoslavia and then, secondly, of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: But in your opinion, there was not an agreement on the governmental level. I'm asking whether this was the case or not. Was there an agreement on the governmental level between the parties?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, but I think you haven't heard my reply very well. When I said the division of power, that concerns governing either municipalities or the state. My answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, I understood your answer very well but I was only asking whether in 1990, there was a governmental agreement or not.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In -- expressed in percentages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: Thank you. You said on several occasions that at this time, tension was rising in Bosnia because of the arrival of Serbian people from Croatia; they were arriving in large numbers. How can you explain this arrival of Serbian refugees?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, they were mentioning the figure of about 100 and then of about a thousand - I never had the precise figure - for Banja Luka. Once they even said that about 5.000 of them had been -- accommodation had been found for them in Banja Luka in the sports hall. There were several thousand of them and so on. So it's very difficult for me to give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many Serbs there were in Bosnia in 1990, and how many there are today?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will provide you with some percentages. As far as I know, there were between about 12 and 18 per cent of Serbs in Croatia. Today, I know that there are -- the percentage is smaller, but I can only give you impressions. I didn't -- I haven't really been involved in this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: Of course, of course. You said that the refusal to obey the mobilisation call created second-class citizens in Bosnia, that is to say those who refused to comply with the mobilisation order at the time Bosnia was part of Yugoslavia, which was a federal state. Were you shocked -- did it seem to you to be shocking to defend federalism against nationalist ideas?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the first question that must be asked is what was the objective of such mobilisation. The first question, in fact, is who is authorised, in accordance with the constitution of the republic, to call for a mobilisation. The second question is why was mobilisation being carried out. This was not the first time that there was a mobilisation in the area of the former Yugoslavia for -- the objective of which was to seize territory, to occupy territory, or the objective of which was to destroy other nations. So each man had to have his own attitude, his own position, if mobilisation was being -- in the case of mobilisation in the municipality of Banja Luka, mobilisation could be called for only by the government, that is to say by the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, mobilisation at the level of the municipality of Banja Luka was considered by us to be illegal. In addition, it contained elements - and this appeared in the public - which indicated it was a mobilisation against the Ustasha. So this mobilisation had, it seems, as an intention a fight against Croats. We mustn't forget that Croatia was an independent state. And even if it hadn't been, it was inconceivable that the people, the masses, should be used to fight other people, other masses, who were only seeking, claiming, their own democratic rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: The federal -- the Yugoslav federal army was in difficulty in Croatia. The barracks had been surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that your questions are touching on the subject that -- about which I can express my opinion, but I am not competent to talk about this. I'm not a historian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm not asking you about your -- about your competence. For the entire period of the indictment, you had a prominent political position in Banja Luka, as you were the president of the SDA. Who were you receiving instructions from?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, the formation of political units, if we are talking about the SDA, was quite spontaneous. It was not really organised. It was a national movement, a people's movement, and although the party was a legitimate one and had been established as a political party, it was a people's movement, and this means that it had all the insufficiencies that come along, that are entailed if it is not well organised. So instructions, instructions for wide-ranging policies, instructions for policies concerning relations within Yugoslavia and concerning international relations, such instructions were non-existent. We had a committee, and certain things were discussed there. There were certain conclusions which were reached, but it was very -- we very rarely discussed about such conclusions at lower levels, except for when we were talking about politics, policies between republics. At a local level, there were such suggestions, and I have to say that I'm not the real person in this case either, because these instructions you are talking about, in 1990, or the first half of 1991, at that time, I wasn't the president. I was the secretary of the party. Mr. Islamovic was the president at the time, and these questions should be addressed to him for that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: That's fine. But I would like to return to your book, your lengthy book, in which you described at length the resistance of the SDA and the problem of Muslims arming, which -- to which you have dedicated many pages in your book. You also spoke about victorious combats such as in Vecici. How were the Muslim forces organised?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait, Mr. Krzic, because I do not have any translation in English any more. And I haven't -- I haven't had interpretation of your last statement, since you started answering this question. I can see the script here on the monitor but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can you hear the interpreter now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear the interpreter now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please be asked to repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krzic, can you repeat what you had just stated? Basically I can read it out for you. No, in fact, I don't even have it in script here. I don't even have it in script here. So -- MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] I can ask my question once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: In the area of Banja Luka, how were the Bosniak armed forces organised? What was their organisation there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have armed forces. As far as we were concerned, the only existing armed force was the one that existed at the time. Again, I am referring to the period of time when I was the president. So we did not have any armed forces in Banja Luka. When you say "forces," I assume that you are referring to some organised units, which did not exist at the time. There must have been -- there were probably groups that I had heard of consisting of 10, 12, 15, I don't know how many, young men who, faced with the very dangerous situation at the time, attempted to protect themselves in such a way. It was quite absurd -- an absurd idea to have any kind of armed force in Banja Luka, which had a very big concentration of soldiers and weaponry in its -- in its barracks. There were about 20.000 soldiers there, plus the population -- the local population that already had weapons. But I know that there were attempts being made by certain individuals to obtain weapons, because if you are surrounded, if you live in a very practical -- practically in a concentration camp, you have to find ways to protect your life. But we did not have armed forces. When you say "armed forces," I assumed that you also refer to the forces that were preparing themselves for some kind of attack. No, there was not such force in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: Yet in your book, you spoke about a person by the name of Smiladzik who at the Banja Luka cemetery counted a certain number of soldiers. And you say that it was a way of recognising Serb losses, which means that there were battles and that there was fighting going on there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you are somewhat mistaken. The figures in question refer to those killed in action at the front line. Every army deems such information to be very useful, and not only useful but also confidential, because every warring faction always tries to conceal such statistics. Those figures referred to the soldiers who had been killed at the front line in Croatia. That was something that was very important for us. And it was also very important for us to find out at which front line such events were taking place. And it was also important for the Serb people to know that there were victims on both sides, because the military junta at that time was trying to hide the number of victims, Serb victims, at the front line, for reasons that you are familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: So the figures referred to Serb soldiers killed at the front line. How far was the front line from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, depends. If you're facing -- if you're looking in the direction of Jajce, the front line was some 70 kilometres away by road, not as the crow flies. But I think that as the crow flies, it would not be not more than 35 kilometres. If you're looking in the direction of Kotor Varos, that would be less than 30 kilometres away. As far as the area of Bihac is concerned, that was a bit further away, perhaps 120 to 150 kilometres away. I believe that I have answered Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Let us try to clarify things. When you speak about the Vecici battle, you mentioned that a number of armoured vehicles, armoured Serb vehicles, were destroyed on the way to the front. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vecici battle was a spontaneous resistance. The area in question had had some terrible experiences with Chetniks in the Second World War, and the local population was aware of the difficult position they found themselves in without weapons, if they didn't have any weapons. So it was a local uprising, local resistance. I know that a number of armoured vehicles, APCs were destroyed. When I say "armoured vehicles," I'm also referring to tanks. But I also mentioned the Air Force, which bombed them with napalm bombs and cluster bombs, which we know are prohibited from the Banja Luka airport. So it is impossible for us not to be on their side, especially in view of the statistics that I had received, a number of murders, rapes that had taken place before the conflict broke out in Kotor Varos. I don't know what you're trying to say, but this was a case of a local uprising, local resistance, and I think that it is a very bright, shiny example of the way people attempted to defend their homes and to resist a form of fascism and aggression. Croats and Bosniaks were fighting on one side, and I believe that there were Serbs among their ranks as well. And the other side -- well, you know who was the other side. The fourth army in the world, in terms of its strength and one of -- and the military -- the local military base was one of the strongest in Europe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. de Roux. Mr. Krzic, I sense in a way that the way we are going might lead us into a confrontation between you and Mr. de Roux, which this Trial Chamber is definitely determined to -- not to let happen. Please try to answer the questions that are put to you without going into other details, unless these are absolutely necessary to explain further the point that you wish to make. But please avoid going into matters which can only provoke further questions and further answers and reactions from you, which would eventually lead us into unnecessary exchange of confrontational remarks. I hope that you have both, Mr. de Roux and yourself, taken the message. And I would invite you to proceed in accordance with what I have suggested. Thank you. Please, Mr. de Roux, go ahead. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't think that this is a confrontation. I'm trying to obtain some clarification. But I believe that the witness could be a bit more succinct in his attempts to provide this explanation to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: Let me go back to something that you mentioned in your testimony, Mr. Krzic. You told us that Vecici was an area where Muslims remembered very well the genocide they experienced in the Second World War. Don't you think that the Serbs in this region also remembered very well the genocide of which they were victims when Bosnia was annexed by Croatia during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not trying to deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to General Talic and what you said about him. You mentioned two occasions on which you met with General Talic. Your delegation was the one of the religious and social organisation or association of local Muslims. You wanted to see General Talic, and he received you. He was accompanied by members of his staff, including Colonel Osman Selak. What was the ethnic background of Colonel Selak?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Bosniak, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: In your book, you mention the fact that you were in constant contact with Colonel Selak, who was a member of General Talic's staff but who, at the same time, according to you, belonged to your network, to your group of resistance. Do you think that General Talic would have kept amongst -- in his ranks Colonel Selak, Colonel Osman Selak, because of this tradition in the army, the multi-ethnic tradition in the former army, or because he was simply mistaken as far as his loyalty was concerned?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to deny what you're saying. I did not have frequent contacts with Colonel Selak. Quite the contrary. On the other hand, it is perfectly clear to everyone that there were Bosniaks and Croats within the former JNA, but it is also clear that, as time went by, the ratio of personnel or staff within the former JNA deteriorated, as regards their ethnic composition. It is common knowledge that Serb nationals were predominant within the past ten years. But let us go back to Colonel Selak. I believe that he will be the best person to describe the situation. I don't see any reason for me to speculate. I can tell you what my attitude is in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to speculate, Mr. Krzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please finish your answer, Mr. Krzic, and try to be as concise as possible. The question was a very direct one and you can answer it in two -- in two sentences, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, but the actual question is -- was to the witness: Why was Colonel Selak kept on by General Talic? How can he say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. "I can't answer the question myself," and we certainly don't have -- but he's definitely not the kind of witness who is not capable of giving the answer that you would have wished or anticipated. I mean, he's a diplomat and he can answer that question very easily.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he's not in a position to answer it, I can think that he can tell us that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think he did. But I merely make the point he was actually being asked what was in General Talic's mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know, Ms. Korner, but let him finish his answer and then you proceed with the next question or another question related to this one. Yes, Mr. Krzic, can you tell us something more about this, and perhaps conclude?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, I cannot tell you what was in General Talic's mind. However, I can tell you that it was my belief that Colonel Selak and other Bosniaks who still existed within the former JNA were the last remnants of this tradition. As far as Colonel Selak is concerned, I think it was his professional attitude that prevailed, because the members of the Army of Republika Srpska were to a large extent dilettantes. However, Mr. Selak was a professional and he -- it would have been very difficult to replace him. I don't know to what extent any personal attitude of General Talic may have played an important role. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my question is very specific. I'm not trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Allow, please, an interval of time between the end of his reply, his answer, and the next question, because of interpretation, for interpretation purposes. Could you please rephrase or put your question again? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, I'm not asking you to tell us what General Talic thought about Colonel Selak. All I wish to know - and I'm basing myself on your book - what was the information that Colonel Selak provided to you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is much more clear. Colonel Selak -- let me try to be as direct as possible. Colonel Selak provided information on several occasions about the prevailing currents within the Army of the Republika Srpska at the time. He also provided some military information, military intelligence, the most important one being about the existence of an air attack against the town of Sarajevo, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: Thank you. As regards other staff officers of General Talic, do you know Colonel Mensud Azutic? Are you familiar with that name?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: When you met with General Talic for the second time, on the second occasion, that is on the 22nd of June - you had asked to see him concerning security problems and security situation in Banja Luka - what was the attitude of General Talic? How did he receive you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that he received us in a correct manner; however, reserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: I will go back to -- I'm now going to go back to what happened on the 22nd of June. You described the meeting as being correct but reserved. But concerning the first meeting which took place in the month of May, you told us that he himself had told you, but that you had also heard that in the corridor -- actually, that he had told the Banja Luka mufti that there might be trouble in Prijedor, and you testified that he had provided you with some important information. How did you use that particular piece of information?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I discussed the information, once we were outside, with Mr. Filipovic, who was also a member of our delegation, because, of course, we were not sure as to what it meant. However, it was our assessment that the information was valuable and that we should check for ourselves what was going on in Prijedor, what the information related to. And as you know, we went to Prijedor to check on the very spot, what was going on, with the local authorities in Prijedor at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: With the president of the Prijedor branch of the SDA, Mr. Mujagic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me? Mr.?

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: It's my pronunciation. Mr. Mujagic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mujagic came later on, but the -- the then president was present. He was later killed. You will have to remind me of his name, which escapes me at the moment, with the then president of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: That is perhaps not important. Apart from these two meetings, you also told us that you had informed General Talic via an American diplomat of the risk of summary executions in Celinac, and you also said that General Talic had sent the military police in order to prevent these executions. What was the relationship with Mr. Kelly, the American diplomat?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I don't quite understand the first part of your question. I don't know which period of time you have in mind. However, I can give you a direct answer to the second part of your question, which I believe is more important, no? Mr. Kelly, as far as I remember, was the second secretary of the American embassy, and in that capacity, he visited Banja Luka on several occasions. He showed interest in the events, and it was easy to communicate with him because he spoke our language, which was an honour for us, I must say, to have such a high-ranking diplomat visit our area, which was, after all, a country. Mr. Kelly didn't ask any questions regarding plans and -- or prospects for the future of Yugoslavia, for example. His questions concerned the local situation. I think that his -- the objective of his visit was to gain some impression as to what was going on. However -- is it okay? I'm sorry, I perhaps have not expressed myself accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was a very simple one. You may be right that the first part of question as put forward to you was not that clear, but the substance of the question was abundantly clear. Counsel for General Talic wanted to know what kind of relationship you had at the time with this Mr. Kelly, the second secretary of the American embassy, who used to pay these visits to Banja Luka. Did you have any kind -- what was the nature of your contacts? Or if there was a relationship between you and this Mr. Kelly, what kind of relationship was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to explain with these two or three sentences what kind of relationship it was. I'm trying to find the right word. It was a friendly relationship, without any commitments, any obligations. I would answer his questions if he -- if he had any. His questions were ordinary questions that one might have expected. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: Yes. But did you ask Mr. Kelly to intervene with General Talic so that executions in Celinac might be prevented?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: Thank you. You then asked General Talic to liberate, to release a certain number of prisoners from the Manjaca prison. Did you achieve that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're now referring to another group of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a different question, and it concerns a different group of people.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not make any personal request. This request was contained in our memorandum. And yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: You also asked that General Talic provide a safe conduct, a travel authorisation for Zagreb. Did you obtain that safe conduct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the request was accepted in principle. The authorisation was given at one point in time, but then it was revoked. It didn't concern me personally but a humanitarian organisation that needed to go to Zagreb. And then the humanitarian organisation in question would have provided the names of people who were supposed to travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: But you yourself did go to Zagreb on several occasions, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never went to Zagreb during the occupation. I was never permitted to do so. I was granted authorisation on one occasion, but it was subsequently revoked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: When did you go to Zagreb, then?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time I went to Zagreb I believe was on the 2nd or the 3rd of April, and I went back on the 6th or the 7th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: It is possible that my memory doesn't serve me right, but you spoke about a trip to Zagreb to negotiate weapons, to procure weapons. When was that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, that was before I went to my company, to the seat of my company, Pliva, to attend one of the meetings. And in a local cafe, I asked a friend of mine if it would be possible to obtain weapons. I meant a piece of -- a weapon for myself. But nothing came of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: Why did you ask for authorisation -- such authorisation or such services from General Talic and not from local civil authorities?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason is a very simple one. You must know that terror reigned in the area, that there were many -- there was a lot of crime going on, and people were not prosecuted or tried. They simply disappeared. There were no courts, properly speaking, for the members of the non-Serb population. And of course that was the reason why we believed that the only hope lied with the -- with the military, the only hope that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: On May 9th, 1992, the general staff of the 1st Army Corps addressed to the crisis staff a request, given the situation, the unsatisfactory security situation. Were you informed of the position of the general staff in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: During the crisis in Banja Luka, a crisis committee had been set up which was set up on the basis of a resolution of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka. And you said that the SDA had been represented at that crisis committee by Emir Djanic. What was Emir Djanic's role within the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, at the beginning it was -- at the beginning, the staff was called differently. The Council of National Defence was its name, and then subsequently, it became a staff. In the National Defence Council -- in fact, this represented a body, a commission, so to speak, which was on the basis of the municipal statute. It was in fact registered in compliance with the statute. And in it, all the parties that won at the elections were to take part. In the National Defence Council, there were representatives of all the parties, including the left wing parties. But as time went by -- and here Mr. Djanic's role was to take part in the workings of the National Defence Council, which was a regular body and which was not formed only in crisis situations. And this was Mr. Djanic's role. As far as I know, Mr. Djanic, as well as other representatives who were not the SDA party, abandoned the National Defence Council, which subsequently became the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: In 1990, two elected persons of the SDA to the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka became -- entered the government. This was Mr. Kuzmic [phoen]. Why in 1992 were they ordered to leave, to abandon the government, and why did they refuse to do so?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the agreement between the parties in power had been -- was being ignored, when it was not being carried out, in many different spheres, and when in fact the practice was quite different, and which I described to you, when not only participation of SDA representatives and representatives of the HDZ was rendered impossible in the different segments of the government -- not only made impossible. They were even made to leave if Bosniaks and Croats were employed there. And when the town was in fact occupied by the Serb defence forces -- it was actually a putsch that was going on. And when our democratic rights were being ignored, that is, the right to propose and appoint, that is, designate, point to the negative events taking place -- when the deputies were being threatened, in many situations we -- and when all this was added up, we felt that the representatives of the SDA in such a government which was basically an SDS government was no longer tenable both from the political point of view -- how can you be in a political government when you have no power at all? Also, from the moral aspect. And that is why we had insisted that they should leave such a government. Moreover, I explained that at the time, tremendous pressure was being exerted on the non-Serb population. It was impossible for us to take part in such a government, given those circumstances, which we in fact informed Mr. Vance and Owen later on about. These two people did not respect the decisions of the executive committee of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: So the only reply that I was expecting was that Mr. Djanic and the other gentleman mentioned remained in the government. Now that you mention Lord Owen and Mr. Vance, during the entire period of the indictment, international negotiations -- an international mission was being conducted to try to find a solution to the Bosnian crisis, to the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You yourself met Mr. Vance and Lord Owen. Can we know what your opinion was of the plan that they had proposed to submit to the different parties concerned?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't meet with them myself. There was a whole team of people involved, where we had representatives of the SDA political party and representatives of our deputy team, that is the president of the deputies group. The Vance-Owen Plan, and similar plans, as far as the SDA party was concerned, could only be discussed within a narrow circle of persons. As regards decisions and positions in that respect, we could only say this to this narrow circle of people, but for more important decisions, a main council, a main board, had to be convened, and the assembly of the party too. So these are matters that had been -- that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were being discussed on a very high level, but what we mentioned from time to time in regard to the plan was something of a practical nature. If governors of so-called cantons was to be -- were to be Serbs, there had to be two deputies of Bosniak -- a Bosniak and a Croat. This was our conclusion because, through that key, we saw a way of protecting the interests of the people, and this we were able to do in this sense in a practical way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: In your book, you mentioned that you had set up a network charged with intelligence work, information work. You were in permanent contact with journalists, with diplomats, with members of humanitarian organisations. To whom were these -- this information, in fact -- to whom was this information intended?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't mention which information, but that doesn't matter. In our work, we were quite transparent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE
utterances.text: To be more precise, throughout the whole record, we examined a number of documents addressed to His Excellency, Mr. Sacirbey, head of the Bosnian mission to the United Nations. How did you think that Mr. Sacirbey would use this information? And would this information be able to exert an influence on the international mediators?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to begin with, information was, of course, submitted to all the international representatives in Banja Luka. All the information at the time, which was sent out abroad from the political aspect, and from the security aspect, the security aspect in respect of the population, all this was sent to all the international organisations, the ICRC, the other humanitarian organisations, to the international observers, and of course, it was only natural that this information be sent to our mission too. Why? Not only for the reason that you yourself mentioned, but because it was impossible to communicate with Sarajevo. Perhaps it's also a question of personal affinity because we believed that when information reached the U.S.A., that it was very highly likely that it would be put to a good use. The U.S.A. are considered to have a principled policy, generally speaking, and especially in respect of conflict situations. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, I have completed my cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Maitre de Roux. It's quarter past ten.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, we cannot hear the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Maitre de Roux. It's quarter past ten. Within 15 minutes, we will break. We will have the usual break. Mr. Ackerman, we can either break now and then you start after the break, or you can start now, stop in 15 minutes' time and then resume after. I'm giving you the option.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It probably makes sense for me to begin now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I don't break everything before I start, I'll start now, please. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krzic. How are you today?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you. I'm keeping well. And you? How about yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm okay. I didn't expect to be talking to you quite this early in the day, but we will begin. You have given a number of statements to investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal, have you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first one was given over a period of time extending from 27 December, 1994, through 23 August, 1995, yes?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It appears that maybe -- that there were about five different sessions with regard to that statement before it was finally prepared and signed by you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expect that was the case. I don't remember all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber why it took so long for that statement to be taken and finished? Were there some problems of any kind? What was the reason it took so long to do that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I cannot explain the reasons, but my impression was that this protracted statement was due to the fact that we kept checking up information. That is how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You mean checking -- the investigators were checking on the information that you were giving them? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was the case. I cannot guarantee that this was so, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was another statement that was given between -- given, actually, on the 24th and the 28th of October, 1999. Do you recall that statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult for me to say so, because I hadn't -- wasn't prepared for this kind of information, that is to say how long the interviews took. This is not what I was told that I would have to say. But all this information has been noted down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ackerman. Ms. Korner, this is precisely what I had in mind to address your attention to this morning, when I said I would imagine that -- or I would expect that there are further documents that ought to be exhibited later on, because these statements were not actually brought forward yesterday or the day before, during the evidence of Mr. Krzic. They were handed to the Trial Chamber, and I also am aware that they had been disclosed to the Defence teams. But unfortunately, we are in a situation now that the witness is being faced with questions relating to these four documents -- four statements that he had made on prior occasions without him having them in front -- in front of him to be able to -- so I think if we can deal with that in a very expeditious manner, it would help the witness to be able to answer. Because he's been referring to dates four, five, six days -- seven days here, eight days there. It's not fair on the witness himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the statements, of course, cannot become exhibits unless by agreement or great chunks of it are put to the witness, in which case an application can be made. But we can provide copies for the witness. And Mr. Ackerman is going to pursue the matter of dates of the statements. Or Your Honour, we can make an admission as to the dates when the statements were made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can start with that first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in any case, if the witness is going to be asked to answer questions on the contents of these statements in particular or events related in these stated statements -- as described in these statements, he ought to have them in front of him. There's no question about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can certainly make -- we would certainly agree the dates that Mr. Ackerman is putting to the witness. If Mr. Ackerman wants to ask further questions, we'll make copies available for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest, Your Honour, that we go ahead and break now, that the Prosecution provide the witness with these statements, because I will question him about them for the balance of this day and probably most of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I take --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm taking that the witness should be provided -- they were written in English, but they've been translated. So for his benefit, he would have to have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the witness has shown us that he understands English as well. And in any case, in the very first part of his evidence on Monday, he did state that he knows English but that he would be obviously answering questions in his own language. So I don't think that should present any problems. And there would be simultaneous interpretation, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Ms. Korner, for you cooperation, and you, Mr. Ackerman, for yours. I think we will break now, and we will resume at ten to -- ten to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I just make certain that they will be provided to him in both languages, because I will want him to refer to the English on occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've got -- I'm assisted by Ms. Karper. We've certainly got the English version here, and we can almost certainly get the Bosnian language one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. So we'll resume at ten to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we now have got versions of the statements both in English and in the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perfect. And the understanding is the following: You are perfectly correct that in the normality of things, these statements would not form part of the exhibits, but if obviously the witness is going to be asked on the contents, then eventually we will definitely have to revise this position and -- because ultimately this Trial Chamber will have to decide also on the credibility of the witness, and that may entail an anticipation of what I am expecting from Mr. Ackerman, some deep exercise. So please call --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say, my understanding is, and it's, I suppose, the common law system but I think it's the same in the United States, as in the U.K. -- as in England, Wales and Your Honour's jurisdiction, is that if large parts of the statement are put in order, as Your Honour says, at the end of the day, to remind yourselves of what was in the statement and of -- to assess the credibility, then the statement will be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, perfect. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, something occurred during the break that just has me -- I can't think of a proper word. "Flummoxed" is the only word that comes to mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that a Texan word?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It may be. On the 13th of December -- and I hope the camera can see this. On the 13th of December, I submitted this box of documents, at the instructions of the Registry, to CLSS for translation. I was given to understand that the people that I used to do translations for me on occasion could not do translations of documents that I might -- that I would seek to use or might seek to use as exhibits in the case, that they had to be submitted to CLSS. There are about 1500 pages of material here that was submitted on the 13th of December. Today, during the break, almost two months later, they are brought back to me with the explanation that nothing has been done with regard to translating them, absolutely nothing, because somebody in the translation department is taking the position that there may be a document or documents in here somewhere that they have already translated in some other case or for the Prosecution in this case. And thus, all this time has gone by, and here I am with documents, many of which I was hoping I could have back in time to use for cross-examination of some of these Banja Luka witnesses, because these are Banja Luka documents. I was labouring under the impression that the matter was proceeding forward normally and properly, only to find today that not a page, not one, has been translated. To my knowledge, there is not one document in here that has been previously translated. It would be foolish for me to submit previously translated documents to them for translation. I wouldn't do that kind of thing intentionally. The other thing that they now want me to do - and I don't mind doing that; I mean, this is a sensible thing - they want me to take the time that it will take me to prepare an itemised index of these documents before I resubmit them for translation. So it will be - I don't know how many days - several days before I'll even have them in the condition that I can submit them back in the form using their itemised index that they want me to use. I was not told, at any time prior to my submission on December 13th, that they would require an itemised index of these documents. I put them together as well as I could. I described them as well as I could. And I submitted a letter on the 13th of December to the translation document, delivered the documents. And the first thing I've heard about them since then was a few moments ago when they were brought back to me in the Defence room. I can't try a case like this. Nobody can try a case like this, when they can't have the materials necessary to defend their client in a very serious genocide case, when they can't have them processed and translated in any kind of a reasonable way. That man sitting over there is entitled to a fair trial. He's absolutely entitled to a fair trial. He's charged with the most serious offence that a person can be charged with. And for the Registry of this Tribunal to sit on these documents for two months without advising me that there was a problem that needed to be solved is unforgivable. And I don't know what the Chamber wants to do about this, and I don't know what the Chamber can do about this, but I've lost two months now. I have to start over again from where I was back on December 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Korner, do you have anything to say about this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, nothing at all. I think all sides have raised the question of the problem with translations a number of times. I don't know that we can assist any. I mean, as Mr. Ackerman says, he's unlikely to have submitted documents which he knows that we've submitted for translation. But without knowing what the documents are, we can't assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I will understand that I will need to discuss this with the other two Judges, and I'll -- we'll come back to you on this matter later on. In the meantime, I think it would help this Trial Chamber to know precisely what kind of documents these are, if you are aware yourself. In other words, what kind of documents are we talking about? I take your words that you consider them necessary for the purposes of cross-examination and also for the Banja Luka chapter, in any case; however, the Trial Chamber would be in a better position to come forward with a better decision if it is made aware of the nature of those documents. In other words, we want to make sure that these are not documents which we can easily do without. This is -- this is what we want.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'll just -- I'll take a moment and give you an example. This binder is full of what we call in the US onion-skin paper documents. They're all originals. They have original signatures. They have original stamps. The stamps are -- the stamps are blue. The signatures are in ink. They are original documents. Every one of these documents comes from the ARK, the Autonomous Region of Krajina. They are signed primarily by Mr. Nikola Erceg, who was the president of the executive committee of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. They are extremely relevant to issues that are going on in this case. The documents are important enough that I did have a significant portion of them translated in rough draft form so that I could have some knowledge of what it is they say. I intend, however, to use all or most of them as exhibits, and so they must be translated officially by the Tribunal before I can do that. With regard to these documents, some of them have already been provided to the Prosecutor in that rough-draft form. I'm in the process of doing that with regard to the rest of them. They're -- to my knowledge -- I'm convinced there is not one document in here that the Prosecution has submitted for translation. There are a number of newspaper articles that have been identified by my staff in Banja Luka as being extremely important to the issues in this case and as being additional to the newspaper articles that have been submitted from that same area by the Prosecutor and tend to provide a more complete picture of what was appearing in the newspapers during the period in question. This stack is a large number of documents that have been secured from various government organs and individuals by my investigative staff in Republika Srpska. I can only rely upon their representation to me that these are extremely important documents for the presentation of our Defence. This is another List of Documents in this package that I can represent have come from a -- an archive of documents kept by someone who was -- and I don't know everything about this particular group, but they're documents that come from the Trnopolje Detention Centre. They're documents that were kept in the regular course of the operation of that Detention Centre during the course of its operation, and they shed a great deal of light upon -- on how that facility operated and how -- I think it's safe to say, although I'm a little reluctant, but I think it's safe to say that they are extraordinarily contrary to what you heard in the opening statement of the Prosecutor regarding the operation of that particular facility. I would not, and will not, submit documents for translation to CLSS that I already have in translation from the Prosecutor or that I think are of no relevance to what I'm trying to do in the defence of this case. I don't operate that way. I'm not that kind of a lawyer. And I don't think there is any history that I have with this Tribunal to cause anybody to believe that I'm that kind of a lawyer. I will defend my client vigorously. I'll defend my client to the absolute best of my ability. And I will work myself ill almost to get that done. But I don't know how to do that if I'm told that I have to do it a certain way, and then when I do it that way, I'm told, "That's still not good enough, and you can't have your documents." I don't know what to do. Maybe we should have a two-month adjournment so I can start this process over again and get these documents done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translations continues] ... Ms. Korner is going to agree with you straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Ms. Korner is going to raise something slightly different, and that is this: Your Honour will recall that we had a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. discussion about disclosure to the Prosecutor of documents that they were aware that they were going to use. It appears from what Mr. Ackerman says that he's aware, obviously because he has Serbo-Croat speakers both on his team and with his client, that he is going to use these documents. Apart from translation problem, I would ask that if these documents will be used, that they be disclosed to us now. It may be that we can assist in some way, in any event, particularly in respect of newspaper articles, because we have sent a number in for translation which haven't come back because they weren't high on the priority list, and we were asked to prioritise our translations. It seems to me that, as Your Honour and we have all discussed before, that the only way to try and get over this in some form is to get what are called draft or not properly authorised translations done by both sides and then, only if there is a real dispute or the document is obviously so important that we ought to have a properly authorised translation, to submit it to CLSS. I regret to say that our information is we have got the same problems as Mr. Ackerman, not quite to the same extent, that the Milosevic trial is taking precedence over everything else in this place, and I think every other trial is falling behind, and that's the real difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that certainly shouldn't carry any weight in the decision that this Trial Chamber will have to take eventually. So I think what you have mentioned is actually the obvious. I mean, I certainly -- and I'm sure that my two colleagues on the Chamber agree with me, without the need to consult them now. This is definitely important. However, there is the time factor. Even if we adopt the solution that you are suggesting, if you are suggesting it, there is still a time factor. We will practically be opening, in the widest terms, the Banja Luka chapter, if we haven't opened it already, very soon. There is a further solution. I mean, there is always the possibility to reserve for the Defence team, both teams obviously, the right to summon back witnesses that would have already given evidence in chief and in cross-examination, if fresh material, fresh evidence, emerges from these documents once they are formally or informally translated. But again, the idea terrifies me. The whole idea having to sit on a moratorium not knowing exactly whether one particular witness is going to be summoned here once, twice, possibly three times, as we go along, and as we have new documents translated, is frightening. So at this point in time, I think my experience tells me to sleep on it for a while, a very short while, discuss it with my two colleagues, and investigate further, within the possibilities that we have, what possible other solutions there could be, and then come back to you, in the spirit you all know it. I appreciate that you both consider this as a problem. You yourself find yourself in the same situation, although not as acute as it is for Mr. Ackerman at the present moment, and it's certainly not a pleasant situation in the eyes of this Trial Chamber or for the purposes of the work that this Trial Chamber has to conduct. I mean, we have the same interest as you both have, that's the pursuit of the truth and justice, and the striking of a balance of the rights, substantial and procedural, of the accused with those of victims and justice in general. But if it is necessary for these documents to play an important part, then we have to find a way, we have to find a solution. So Mr. Ackerman, I will, of course, give you the floor again but this is what I intend doing. I intend to take my time, me and the other two Judges on this Trial Chamber, and face the issue again, the problem again, with a concrete solution. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a couple of things. I have a suggestion and a comment. First a comment. I had felt that I was not in -- on good ground, I guess is the way to put it, to -- at this stage in the case, since I only submitted these two months ago, to complain that I didn't have material translated that I could use for cross-examination of witnesses that are coming up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is something that, in my mind, the Tribunal, the Chamber, could throw back in your lap.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go to something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I do want to tell you about that is that the only documents that I have -- most of these documents I've not had before I -- a few days before I submitted them. The other thing that -- my suggestion, and it would require the aid of the Chamber, I think, for this to work. I have two people ready, willing and able to sit down and spend significant hours doing translations of these documents. They are highly competent. They do excellent work. But they have been told by the Registry of this Tribunal, that they are not permitted to do translations of documents that are destined to become or could become exhibits before the Tribunal. That is -- I understand that to be a rule of the Tribunal that is somewhat sacrosanct. If that rule can be relaxed because of the expediency of what we are trying to do, I have no problem with that. I would submit these to them tomorrow and get this process going. If I have to go through CLSS, then it's going to take me a lot longer. It's going to take us all a lot longer. So if you can aid me in that regard, it would be very much appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will go into that and see if that could be done. I know that there is something cooking that would streamline, more or less, the practice as far as which documents ought to be translated and which documents -- or not exactly which documents ought to be translated but an order of precedence. But I can't give you more information on that. I think we need time, as you would understand, to try and not only to discuss it amongst ourselves, because this is not something that we can discuss here and now. We require time. And we also, I think, have to find out exactly what possibilities there are. You have my word, we will come back to you as quickly as possible. This is not something to be taken lightly. I am unfortunately very much aware that the system that this Tribunal -- that prevails in this Tribunal is problematic in itself, because -- even as far as the Prosecution is concerned. I mean, they may come tomorrow morning with the good or bad news that they have just come across some fresh information, and as I understand it, with the discussions that we have had, not I or those present, I mean all the Judges, we are made aware of this and that this constitutes a big problem, a major problem, because evidence comes in in the course of a trial which may be fundamentally important. And so when I said I could throw back those documents on your lap, saying -- I mean, you can't expect miracles to happen from the 13th of December to date. At the same time, I mean, if there was a problem in having those documents translated, there was no reason on earth why you weren't told so at the -- then, if not necessarily on the same day. I know that there was a Christmas recess but certainly no justification for that. But anyway, we will go into it. We'll see what can be done. I appreciate that you have not tried to make a divisive issue out of this, that you see the problem and that you are cooperating with the Trial Chamber. I appreciate that. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the only thing, though is -- because I said something else. We are making a formal request for disclosure to us of documents that Mr. Ackerman now knows, whether translated or not, he's going to be using.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour requires that I make disclosure of any document that I intend to use as an exhibit in the case, as evidence in the case. And I will comply with the rule, absolutely completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As soon as I know that I'm going to use a document as an exhibit, I will give it to the Prosecutor. I'm in the process of giving them documents right now. It's just that with everything else I've been doing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But from the way -- let's -- from the way you tried to explain the importance and relevance of those documents, I understood that it is certainly not your intention to -- not to use those documents. It's certainly your intention to make use of those documents and fully so. Because one set of the documents come from the ARK crisis. One set of documents were given to you from or were collected by your investigators from I can't remember where. And you attached so much importance to those documents that you've managed to convince the Trial Chamber here and now that it is certainly a set of documents that we ought to take -- give serious consideration to in the light of what your complaint was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So certainly I was not understanding that you still had doubts as to whether you would be making use of those documents. If I was reading your mind's -- your mind and your lips well, you certainly were referring to documents that you are going to make use of, and full use of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I suspect that I will. When I haven't read them, it's difficult for me to make that decision. If they are what they were represented to me to be, then, yes, I'll be using them. But I don't know that they are until I look at them. I will say that I have received documents that they weren't exactly what they were represented to be. But I'll go through them as quickly as I can, because apparently I'm going to have to index them in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I now have someone who can help me and look at them and tell me what they say. And I can make rather quick decisions about whether I'm going to use them or not. And I will make disclosure as quickly as I can, I really will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. So perhaps we could bring in the witness. Yes. Mr. Krzic, you will continue now being cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman. Of course you don't need to make the solemn declaration again. We take it that you will continue your evidence on that same declaration that you entered before. You may sit down. Thank you. I suppose we better make available the documents that were referred to earlier immediately to Mr. Krzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just wondering, does Mr. Ackerman want him to have all of the statements together or just one at a time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All of them. Okay. Your Honour, they've been marked. So the English version and the date is shown. And then next to it is the Bosnian version. And there are four statements. They've been numbered "1" through to "4."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Chronologically, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Backwards, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Krzic, welcome back. We were speaking about what I believe is the statement that the Prosecution has numbered as number 2. That would be your statement of 24 and 28 October, 1999. Would you see if you can find that one, please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The statement indicates that there were interviews on the 24th of October and the 28th of October. There was a three-day break between those sessions, the 25th, 26th, 27th. Can you tell the Chamber why there was a three-day break there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as regards the schedule of the investigation team, I think that it was their position that was decisive in this manner. I've never thought about it. I don't know why there were breaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would that be true with the breaks in the other two statements that you gave, that you really don't know why there were gaps in the times that they talked to you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do remember that there were reasons given to me for that. I believe that they had something to do with the obligations and commitments that they had in the relevant country. I was probably not the only witness that they interviewed at the time, so I assume that perhaps those were the reasons for these gaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Throughout this period of time when you were -- from 27 December 1994 until 29 August 2001, which apparently was your last statement, the last day you spoke with them, were you provided any kind of financial or other assistance by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you have had a chance to review all of these statements after coming here to The Hague in preparation for your testimony in this case. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't insist on reviewing the statements. I received a copy each time, and it was -- I was able to decide whether to review it or not. But because every statement was signed by me, I didn't think it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question, then, is: Have you reviewed them in recent days in preparation for the testimony you've given here?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean in recent days? During my stay here in The Hague or -- I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know how long a period of time you were involved in preparing for your testimony here. But during that preparation time, however long it was, did you review these four statements?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here in The Hague, no. But of course I have all these statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you prepared at this point, as you sit here under oath, to swear to this Trial Chamber that every statement made by you in each of these four statements is absolutely true and correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not once did I fail to speak the truth in my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you, in your review of the statements, found any translation problems? I assume you reviewed them both in English and your native language. Have you found any translation problems that you would like to bring to our attention?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I usually had the translation in my language, and I never felt the need to check the translation because I trust the interpreters. But also, I must say that I'm not an expert in the English language. I don't know it sufficiently well so as to be able to make any suggestions, especially in cases of some nuances and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention now to the first statement that you gave, the one given over that period of several months in 1994 and 1995. Would you find that and get it in front of you, please?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you would look at what in the English version is the second page, the statement indicates that you were granted an FAO scholarship to Copenhagen in 1975. Can you tell me what an FAO scholarship is?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I applied for an FAO scholarship. It is a scholarship which covers the area of agriculture, generally speaking, and in my case, the area in question was meat processing industry, or more specifically meat products. I don't know whether it is necessary for me to explain in further detail. I can do it, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question is what is FAO? What does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Food and Agricultural Organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was an organisation of what entity or government or country?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is part of the organisation of United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So the scholarship was actually provided to you by a division of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
