utterances.text: Indirectly, yes, because it was provided by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which acted as a representative of a state agency which was called Technical Assistance or something like that, and it was through that particular agency that we applied for scholarships such as the FAO scholarship.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. de Roux began his questioning of you, Mr. Krzic, with a question about the goals of the SDA. You remember being asked that question, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you indicated that one of the objectives was to help the development of democracy in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It follows from the provisions of the statute of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To work toward the development of a democratic society? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, it is my -- my interpretation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was your understanding of what the goals of the SDA was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And as president, those were goals that it was your job to try to put into reality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask what you meant on page 4 of your statement - and I don't know where to find it in the Serbo-Croat version but the English version, at the bottom of page 4, it reads: "We Bosniaks" - speaking of the development of the SDA party - "We Bosniaks had the first possibility to express our nationality for 70 years."

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Could you tell me which -- [Interpretation] Which paragraph are you referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's under a section called, "Banja Luka SDA." It's on page 4 of the English version, halfway through.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see. I found it. Thank you. Thank you. What was your question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What were you -- what was your meaning, what were you intending to convey, when you said, with regard to the SDA, "We Bosniaks had the first possibility to express our nationality for 70 years"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, during the so-called first Yugoslavia, if I may call it that way, we did not have the right to declare ourselves as Bosniaks. During the second Yugoslavia, in Mrkonjic Grad, at the meeting which took place in 1943, which was a meeting where -- attended by the representatives of all ethnic groups of Yugoslavia, as far as I know, it was during that meeting that their nationality was recognised. But practically speaking, during the communist Yugoslavia, we did not have the right to refer to ourselves as Bosniaks. We were granted that right only later on, although in the meantime - and I'm sure you are aware of that - we were given the right to use the term "Muslims." And that is the reason why I described that period of time the way I did, and the reason why I felt that it was only then that we were given the right to use the term "Bosniaks," which is something that had belonged to us as citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina for ages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you weren't permitted to use the term "Bosniaks" until the creation of the SDA? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not, no. Of course, it was possible to use the term unofficially, but officially, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was there some kind of a law that prohibited you from calling yourselves Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that you know that during the times of the communist Yugoslavia, we had three possibilities in Bosnia and Herzegovina to declare ourselves in terms of nationality - Croat, Serb, Yugoslav - and yes, there was a fourth possibility, as not declared. A huge number of Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina chose not to declare themselves or to declare themselves as Yugoslavs. Again, I wish to emphasise that I'm not a politician and I have not prepared myself for this subject, but it was only sometime in 1955 or even later that we were given the right to declare ourselves as - no, I think I'm mistaken; it was even later than that - as Muslims. So we often declare ourselves as Muslims, although it was not a traditional, historical term, and in my opinion, it was an unnecessary way of avoiding the use of the term "Bosniaks." I still don't see the reasons for that, because the term "Bosniak" is a traditionally acceptable term, whereas any religious affiliation is not relevant when we are speaking about citizenship and nationality and the fact of belonging to one particular country or state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you'd agree with me that at least by the time of the 1974 constitution, that you had been -- you were able to declare yourselves as Muslims, at least.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But we were not consulted on this term. There was no referendum organised for that purpose. We did not even have adequate representatives who would have been our deputies and who would have advocated our interests in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, in 1974, the key system was in effect. There was proportional representation of all of the nationalities of Yugoslavia in the assemblies. You had a number of deputies in the assemblies that reflected the population -- the Muslim population of Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. That had been the case with Yugoslavia since its creation following World War II. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I have already stated that the Communist League made sure that at least in terms of names or ethnic background, all ethnic groups be represented in a proportional way. However, very often attention was paid only to the name of the individual in question, not to his background or his convictions. And as you probably know, two individuals of two different ethnic groups could have the same name. Such cases were also possible. But if it was all just a great show, it was the way things looked like, the way they seemed. But to a certain extent, it was satisfactory. One could be satisfied with the state of affairs to a certain extent, because again, to a certain degree we were given possibility to express our views.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that what you meant when you made the statement we're referring to, "We Bosniaks had the first possibility to express our nationality for 70 years," is it your testimony that all you're talking about there is that you had the right to call yourselves -- finally after 70 years, to call yourselves Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had in mind the fact that even during the Austro-Hungarian times, the Bosniaks had the right to use the term "Bosniak." However, after the Kingdom of Yugoslavia was created and during the communist years, they did not have that right. And that was the period of time that I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You recall, I'm sure, the census that was conducted in 1981. How were the Muslim people permitted to identify themselves in that census in 1981?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the majority -- again, I'm really reluctant to mention any statistics. It would go beyond my competence. I would like to leave it to experts. But it is true that the majority of Bosniaks identified themselves as Muslims ever from the first census that gave them that option.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next sentence after you say, "We Bosniaks had the first possibility to express our nationality for 70 years," in the next sentence you say: "We considered it a chance given to us by the West." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you answer the question, Mr. Krzic, may I ask you, Mr. Ackerman, what are you trying to prove by this series of questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm trying to find out, Your Honour, what he means when he makes these statements, what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But for the purpose of this trial, what's the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. The relevance is -- is his credibility, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Mr. Krzic, answer this question, and then we'll see about the other questions that may be following.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I am merely expressing my opinion here. And then you must be aware of the fact that this was all written in a book which was perhaps written without recourse to adequate and reliable information. What I had in mind when I said that was the fact that the issue of ethnic or national affiliation had long been solved in the West. The way it was solved did not endanger or threaten anyone. All ethnic groups were allowed to express themselves socially, politically, and culturally. And it was that freedom of expression that I had in mind when I said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go to another issue now. On Monday, in this room, you were asked by Mr. Koumjian about your tenure as president of the Banja Luka SDA. And your answer from the transcript about how you left the leadership of the Banja Luka SDA was as follows: "Several members of the Executive Council of the SDA in Banja Luka and some of the deputies of the SDA of Banja Luka convened a meeting in Sarajevo. And during that meeting, the leadership of the party was entrusted with a different person." Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ackerman. Yes, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just ask as a procedure to be followed by both sides that when a transcript is quoted, for the sake of the Trial Chamber and opposing counsel, we could cite the page so that we could go to it and find what counsel is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Your observation is perfectly correct. And Mr. Ackerman is kindly invited to state whether he is referring from the official -- or an official transcript - because until now, it will still be unofficial - and what page he is reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 1414, Your Honour, line 16 through 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. And thank you, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you this request: How was it that the leadership was entrusted to a different person at that point? Were you a candidate?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the explanation is a simple one. I was already in the state service, in the public service. I was working in London. And I was not able to work in the -- to participate in the work of the party. I was a professional then. And to perhaps present party's views or an organisation was unacceptable for me at the time, if that is what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So did you advise this group of people, then, in some way that you had no interest in continuing as president of the Banja Luka SDA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I took advantage of my visit to Sarajevo to bring together members of the -- other members of the executive council, and to see that something be done in, in fact, animating the work, activating the work, of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And at the same time, you resigned as president of the SDA in Banja Luka, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In practical terms, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you look, please, at the -- in the English version, it's the last paragraph on page 5, and the last two lines of that paragraph, where you say in your statement, "In 1993, I was secretly elected president of the regional board of the occupied territories of Bosanska Krajina." Do you find that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have a number of questions about that. What do you mean when you say you were secretly elected?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the agreement was within the executive council of the SDA. I mentioned this. Perhaps you have failed to realise what I said, that we should formally proclaim ourselves in Banja Luka as a regional board of the SDA, because members of the boards in other towns were either escaped or were killed. We believed that we could only be protected - perhaps this was not the right way of thinking - but we believed that we could be at least partially protected from arrests and from being killed if we had higher political functions. That is to say, when we -- if we were to be arrested, that we could inform the international public and that this and that person was arrested, and add to this his function in the SDA, and also mention that he was one of the vice-presidents of the regional board. In my case, it was said that I was also president of the regional board of the SDA. It was believed that this would attract international reaction if their position were to be mentioned. This was not legally a valid act, but those were the conditions we were living in within a concentration camp, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me go back to the question I asked you. Are you looking at the transcript there on your screen? Do you see the transcript on your screen, Mr. Krzic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am -- I occasionally glance at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question I asked you was: "What do you mean when you say you were secretly elected?" I must ask you that again. What do you mean, "secretly elected"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't -- did not render this public through the press or any other media. We wanted to avail ourselves of this only in instances where we might be arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, when you speak, then -- thank you. I appreciate that. When you speak of the occupied territories of Bosanska Krajina, what specifically did you consider to be the occupied territories of Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was the territory controlled by the Serb army, or the Army of the Republika Srpska, the so-called Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I assume that you would, for instance, put the Banja Luka municipality in that category?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So, in effect, what you did, then, in 1993 was create a regional organisation of the SDA party, or a sort of SDA autonomous region, secretly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, these were not representatives of the people. These were deputies, a group of people who, in a small room, decided that this was the right way to act in order to save their lives. We did not make this public, but the explanation, as you can see from the document, was sent to our SDA members, explaining to them why we were doing that, and simply to say to the journalists, "This is a political official and let us have him saved." This was something intended for the press, because it would not be possible to have interventions for every individual person in Banja Luka. We had no other goal before us, neither verbally or in writing, nor formally. Self-declaration of the members of a non-existing political body, doing so to save our lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to take you to a new subject now, on page 13 of your statement, and that would be the English version. If you look at the very bottom, the last paragraph, about halfway through that last paragraph, you say, "There is no doubt" -- and you're speaking of a time when you had been arrested. You say, "There is no doubt that the CSB leadership knew that I was in the CSB building and that I was being interrogated and tortured." You see that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who was the CSB leadership that you were speaking of there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this, first of all, was in the building of the CSB, that is in the SUP building where the security services were accommodated. I was convinced that the head of that service, as -- and of the SUP as a whole, was Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And who else was the leadership? You seem to be speaking in plural here, not just one person.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember other individuals, that is his assistants, if you're referring to them. I could not quote their names. But when I was referring to the leadership, I had in mind the lower-ranking officers, because such an information could not just pass unnoticed. It would have been heard straight away, and I mentioned this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you used the term "CSB leadership," what you were referring to was the lower-ranking officers of the CSB?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and on a higher level, too, the higher-ranking ones as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What information do you have -- I mean, you say there is no doubt. What information do you have that higher-ranking leadership persons of the CSB were aware that you were there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because one of the police officers - who was indeed an officer - were present when I was arrested, and once I even asked him to inform one of the ex-SDA leaders, that is the lawyer, Mr. Bojanic, which he accepted to do. And these were policemen. And as you know, the news spread through the town and it was impossible for this piece of news not to be known. And this piece of news was also transmitted through the international news systems which were listened to carefully. Finally, during the torture and the whole procedure, I was also told quite openly that even Karadzic knew about my arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. But the sentence that I referred you to: "There is no doubt that the CSB leadership knew that I was in the building and I was being interrogated and tortured," you're referring to the present tense there. You're saying at the time you were there, there's no doubt that they knew you were there. I'm not asking about afterwards. I'm asking about at the time that you were there. What proof do you have that Stojan Zupljanin, for instance, knew that you were there being tortured and interrogated? What proof do you have of that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, policemen were present who were observing me through the window. They were on duty. And they watched me when two soldiers took me to the sports hall to beat me up, and they were present all the time when I was being helped to stand up. These were military police members, and it was impossible for them not to have informed their superiors of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zupljanin was not the superior of military police, was he?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer these questions exactly because I don't have the documents to base myself on. But there was -- it was generally known that any event of this kind could not pass unnoticed by Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it's your position, then, is it, that you're able to say that there is no doubt that he knew of your presence there at the time you were there because you were being observed by some police officers? To you, that's enough to prove that there's no doubt that he knew about it; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the torture went on the whole day in the SUP building and as policemen went upstairs and downstairs, there were lots of policemen and lots of soldiers that were doing that, it was quite logical for me to conclude that they knew. The soldiers were shouting amongst each other, "Do you know what sort of person we caught," and even mentioned me. So it was quite public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. I think it's time to move to something else. I think he has answered this question abundantly clear to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm moving, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At the very bottom of the page, you describe yourself as a "man who had stood up against the Chetniks." Now, I assume you're talking about that period of time and not the Chetniks from World War II.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I must refer to the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't have to apologise for doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I would just explain. I believe that the page numbering may be different, because this first statement was done in a different font that's no longer on our computers. I know that when I printed it out, I have different page numbers than Mr. Ackerman has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case, we're talking about the same paragraph, so there shouldn't be great difficulties. The same paragraph, Mr. Krzic, from which Mr. Ackerman had read the short sentence regarding the CSB leadership. It's further down, two sentences further down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have problems to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The heading of the section, Mr. Krzic --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've found it. I've found it. You asked something about Chetniks. I apologise. Could you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The statement you made was -- let me give you the whole sentence so that you'll have it in context. "I absolutely think that the CSB leadership was informed from the beginning, otherwise they would have killed me immediately." And then the phrase I'm interested in: "As I was a man who had stood up against the Chetniks." What do you mean that you were a man who had stood up against the Chetniks? What Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I spoke about the crimes publicly. It was publicly recognised by the perpetrators of the crimes that they were called Chetniks. They were called Cetnika kums, vojvodas, and that they follow the Chetnik tradition. I spoke about the crimes that they had committed quite openly, and I can conclude that I would have been liquidated immediately if they were to -- had decided about my fate. The soldiers surrounding me often said that they were that, and I think that I have a right to draw that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian was asking you during your testimony, I think on Monday, about various dismissals in Banja Luka of non-Serb people between April and December of 1992. And one of the group that you informed us had been dismissed from their positions were most non-Serb judges. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that dismissals also included people working in the judiciary, and I said that non-Serbs were dismissed. But I also said that in some cases, that Serbs were also affected by this because they may have been from mixed marriages. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The SDA party was a party that represented approximately 13 or 14 per cent of the population of the Banja Luka municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It represented 13 to 14 per cent of the electorate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know of a judge who was appointed in 1991 by the name of Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What was Judge Jankovic's nationality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this candidacy for appointment to a judicial position was supported by the SDA party, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim that this was so. The only thing that I can remember with regard to that election, that some members of the SDA objected to him. But whether they voted or not, it is difficult for me to say at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me refer you to page 18 of your report. Not your book. Not your book, your report, the first one we've been referring to, page 18.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The English version; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's the English version.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: About halfway down, there is a paragraph which begins with the name, Mr. Jankovic. Within that first sentence, you say, "Mr. Jankovic asked for the support of the SDA. He received this support and was appointed to the Basic Court."

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this with some conviction, but not 100 per cent convinced.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, when we started today, I asked you if everything contained in your statements, that you would swear to as the truth, and you said, "Absolutely, everything is the truth." So that must be the truth, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. That's argumentative to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Don't you think that the objection ought to be sustained?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it probably should be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I would have sustained it in your position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. So you don't need to answer that question, Mr. Krzic. And Mr. Ackerman will put the next few questions before we break again, unless he prefers to stop here and continue later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I'll maybe have one or two more, Your Honour, to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So this is a -- this is a fact that you have pointed out in your statement that you are now saying you're not quite certain about?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you please, I gave this statement in reference to a relevant event, and that is the massacre in Vlasic, so that when describing the judge who attended the investigations in Vlasic, I was asked what I knew about the Judge Jankovic, and I stated what I knew. I didn't speak an untruth, a falsehood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, in fact, the point you were making, Mr. Krzic, was that Mr. Jankovic, as the investigating judge, regarding what happened at Mount Vlasic, even though he had the title of judge --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I haven't finished the question. Even though he had the title of judge, did not act independently because he was under the control, de facto, of Mr. Zupljanin. That's the point you were trying to make, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to say that according to my information. And you know I'm not a lawyer. I never worked in state institution of that kind. To my mind, the investigating judge, on the basis of the customs in practice in the state services, he was supposed to have come out on the site of the crime, but the situation in Banja Luka was such at the time that he couldn't have done this without consulting the most responsible police officers. There was a situation where one's own regulations were not respected, and he could have been ordered not to go. That is my opinion. And everyone would have obeyed because if he did not obey orders, in those days, this was a very dangerous thing to do. I believe, and as far as I can remember - I'm not an expert in that matter - the public prosecutor was the one who issued orders under the old communist system. If, in the meantime, state regulations changed, regulations that had to do with subordination, I'm not aware of that. But it is impossible that he would have gone to the site of a massacre against the non-Serbs, unless he had the consent of superiors, unless of course he was an exceptionally brave person, willing to risk his own life, but then again the consequences would have been quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we can break now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a break of 25 minutes. We will resume at five to 1.00, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to raise two short administrative matters at the end of the proceedings. So if Mr. Ackerman perhaps could just give me five minutes, it really will be short. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. Please admit the witness again. Yes, Mr. de Roux. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before the witness arrives, I would like to say that I have spoken with General Talic about the defence, because I won't be here on the 13th, Wednesday the 13th, and he would like Ms. Natasha Fauveau to be co-counsel and be present in his place -- in his name. I'm talking about Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's forget about the formality, whether she can be co-counsel or not co-counsel, because she cannot be a co-counsel or described or accepted as co-counsel, because she isn't according to the records of this case. But if there is this declaration, which I would like General Talic himself to make as well, to the effect that he has no objection in being represented on Wednesday when we meet next by Ms. Fauveau, then I will have it on record. But not to have her described as co-counsel, because you -- unfortunately, you cannot. As I said, when you were absent, Ms. Fauveau did a fantastic job. So it's definitely -- definitely General Talic was very ably represented. Yes. Mr. Krzic, you may sit down, please. Yes. General Talic, you have heard what Mr. de Roux, your chief counsel, has just stated. THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no objections to being represented by Ms. Natasha Fauveau, and I agree to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So Mr. Ackerman, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, before the break, we were near the bottom of page 18 of your statement. You say there -- it's about one, two, three, four -- the sixth line up from the bottom, with regard to this issue that you were discussing about Judge Jankovic and how he couldn't actually perform the duties that a judge constitutionally should perform in that situation. You said that at the time, referring to this period of time: "There was one constitutional system and one de facto system." And that is the case, isn't it, that you couldn't always determine who was in charge and who had power based upon the title they had or the position they held? There was a de facto power system that had grown up during this period of time.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But not in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Specifically in certain situations, however, that was the case, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain cases, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me take you now to the next page. You have a section of your report that is under the heading "Mr. Brdjanin." You say at the end of the first paragraph, that, referring to Mr. Brdjanin: "His father was a war criminal during World War II." What proof do you have of that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well known among who?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was well known among the citizens, even those of Celinac. It was well known that his father had been punished as a Chetnik in the course of the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you go to the second page, at the top, first full paragraph -- first paragraph, you indicate that Mr. Brdjanin became a member of the Banja Luka assembly. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could we ask, Mr. Ackerman, are you referring to page 20, first full paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 20, English. It's not the first full paragraph. It's the paragraph at the top of the page, about halfway through.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you find that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you having difficulties, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, were you asking me? I found it. I found the passage. I didn't realise that you had asked me this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's true, is it, that he was a member of the assembly of the Banja Luka municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now, I can't say this for sure, because in the Banja Luka Dom Kultura, Centre of Culture, which is where municipal sessions were held, sessions were held at the various levels. Assembly sessions were held at various levels there. So there was a question concerning Mr. Brdjanin, who was in Banja Luka. The question was whether he could be a member of that assembly. And that was a period during which we no longer participated in the work of the Banja Luka assembly. So our information on certain appointments or elections was limited. I was thinking of the fact that he was a member of the assembly of Republika Srpska, and as far as I know, he was also a member of the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question I asked you about was, you said that he was a member of the assembly of Banja Luka. Have you learned since you gave that statement that that's not true? Or do you still believe that to be true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that Mr. Brdjanin moved to Banja Luka in that period. It's possible that certain elections were held. So it's possible that he was there. I would often see him there. I even saw him before, before this period. So this is an impression I had, not only with regard to him but also with regard to certain other people. I can't say this for sure because I don't have any documents here. I can't say for sure whether someone was or was not a member of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you're looking at a statement that you signed, and you don't say that he was possibly a member of the Banja Luka assembly. You say that he was, don't you? You don't say, "It's possible that he was," or, "I thought maybe he was," or, "He could have been." You say he was, as a statement of fact, in a statement that you signed; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If you go down to the next paragraph that starts with the name "Mr. Brdjanin," you said in your statement, "He was always the strongman, prepared to do everything Dr. Karadzic or others wanted him to do." Right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could I ask the registry to provide the witness with Prosecution Exhibit 34B and 34A?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, I'm going to tell you what I have asked that you be shown are shorthand notes of a meeting of the deputies club of the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina, held in Sarajevo on 28 February, 1992. I want to draw your attention to page 36 of the English version, and I don't know where the same language would appear in the Serbo-Croat version, the B/C/S version. I will tell you that the person who is speaking is Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hold on a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I understand where the question is going, I'm going to object on the basis of relevance. I believe Mr. Ackerman would argue this goes to the witness's credibility, because I presume he's going to show some split between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Brdjanin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, obviously. But I just can't see why your objection ought to be sustained. It's definitely relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Because Mr. Krzic was not present and would not have had access to those documents at the time he made the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what? He's making a blanket statement with regard to Mr. Brdjanin in this particular statement, saying that Mr. Brdjanin is the kind of political strong animal -- I'm using the term "animal" not as -- we use it to describe a pure politician -- who as part of his policy has taken to follow exactly and always everything that Mr. Karadzic demands or expects from him. So if now we are coming to the stage of having a witness confronted with statements, public statements, made by Mr. Karadzic and others, I think of course there is a relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's the issue. It's not a public statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Of course it's relevant. He's going to be asked -- I mean, he's on cross-examination, and he will definitely be asked whether he will sustain or maintain the statement that he had made in the first place with regard to Mr. Brdjanin. I mean, it's perfectly legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm not going to argue the point further. I see I'm losing it, so I'll sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm asking you to look at page 36 of the English version. And I think you have found that page. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the English version. But once again, as these are sensitive issues, I would like to find the same passage in Bosnian. But if you tell me what you want, maybe I wouldn't have to look for the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to the statement made by Dr. Karadzic with regard to Radoslav Brdjanin at this time. The English translation reads: "We can and we must renounce everyone who refuses to work the way we have agreed, Brdjo and all the rest. When Brdjo appears somewhere, he's like a bomb. He blows up everything. Then he winks at him. And I won't allow it as a psychiatrist and as the party leader." Skipping a paragraph: "He's crazy. He's not normal," Dr. Karadzic continues. "He doesn't know what he can do and what he can't do." You see that language there, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic as a psychiatrist is criticising Brdjanin, calling him crazy, saying he's not normal; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what is stated here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you said after that, after he had called him all these things and said all these things about him that, "Mr. Brdjanin was prepared to do everything Dr. Karadzic or others wanted him to do." Don't you think that's a bit unlikely?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now I can anticipate what your objection is. And it's going to be sustained. I think you ought to -- I dispense you from having to explain it, because I know exactly what -- Mr. Ackerman, I would suggest to you to rephrase your question. And I know -- and you ought to know exactly along which lines. I mean, he made a statement way back in 1995, a statement that you read out to him. Now you have read out to him what Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic had stated during that meeting of the deputies club. The obvious question is whether he would like to maintain the statement that he had made on that previous occasion or whether he would prefer to revise it, but -- or something along those lines. But not the way you've phrased it in the beginning, anyway. Whether he still believes that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you stand by your statement, Mr. Krzic, that Brdjanin was ready to do the will of Dr. Karadzic any time he was asked to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a certain time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you understand, do you not, that the statement that we just read about Dr. Karadzic calling him crazy was in February of 1992, preceding all of the events that are part of the allegations in this indictment? You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know something else too. There are such turnarounds in politics. Sometimes enemies become your best friend, and sometimes people who spoke very ugly things about others turn around and say very positive things. So your statement is quite relative, as is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A little further down in the same paragraph, the last sentence of that paragraph on page 20 of your statement, referring to Brdjanin: "He was the right person to organise ethnic cleansing, camps, and deportation." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any proof at all -- and when I say "proof," I mean something more than what you think. Do you have any proof at all that Mr. Brdjanin ever organised ethnic cleansing or organised any camps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, this, I will not allow you to put this question, because this is obviously a personal judgement of another person. It's not a question of whether he has proof or not proof. This is what at the time Mr. Krzic was making a statement believed. It's not a question of whether he has proof or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my only point is that he made the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And my question is whether it's true or not. I think it's not. I want to ask him if he can justify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can only ask the witness whether he believes that statement to be true but not what evidence or what proof he has that Mr. Brdjanin was the right person for -- to commit all these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I ask him, Your Honour, if he has any justification beyond personal animus for having made the statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, of course not. That's even worse. That's even Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. worse. I mean, I notice that you skipped the previous sentence. And I can understand why you skipped it, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me find it. Maybe I won't skip it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "He is a man of hatred, of so little knowledge and narrow perspective that he had no possibility to create anything constructive." Is that the one you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I mean, he is telling the interviewers what is his personal assessment of Mr. Brdjanin is, and that's it. You definitely know, as an experienced lawyer, Mr. Ackerman, that we are not going to condemn anyone because one witness believes that that person is capable of organising camps, deportation and whatever. What we will need is evidence, not opinions or judgements on other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me just ask this question, then, Mr. Krzic, about that entire paragraph which begins, "Mr. Brdjanin," and ends, "morbid type." What you're expressing there to the investigators is your personal opinion of Mr. Brdjanin; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal opinion is based on certain facts, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I ask you a question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have come across this several times before, Mr. Krzic, and my answer has always been no. You're here to answer questions and not to put questions. I won't even --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's just that I omitted to say that Mr. Karadzic actually confirmed my views.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want to explain further, but very concisely, what you mean, yes, but that's about it, and you're not entitled to put questions to Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's no problem. I mean, I don't need apologies. Just go ahead. If you have a further statement to make, please go ahead and make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he wants to ask me questions after the close of our session today, I won't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No possibility of a dispensation here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I didn't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. So let's go ahead and not waste time, because we are wasting precious time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'll move.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, between April and December of 1992, you were making efforts to inform the world about the things that were happening in Banja Luka, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And to be able to do that, you made efforts to keep yourself aware of the things that were happening in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You paid close attention to television and the radio and the press.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, one moment, because I am not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say "close attention," yes, but I must qualify the statement because it was not always possible for me to follow the media, because of frequent power shortages and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Watching TV and sometimes listening to the radio was difficult because there was no electricity a lot of the time; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How often during 1992 was the electricity non-existent?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is almost impossible to answer that question. The question can only be answered by the person who was in charge of power distribution. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you said, and I can find it by next week, but you said at one point, I think, that you were -- it was very rare that you were able to run your fax machine because the power was off so much. So it was off more than it was on; isn't that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speculate. Perhaps it was 50/50.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And that wasn't just for non-Serb residences but it was for the entire city of Banja Luka; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exclusively, because there were certain areas of the town which were more frequently cut off than others. Whether that was on purpose or by coincidence, I don't know, but it was not uniform. That's what I'm trying to say. The centre of the town was better supplied with electricity than the outskirts of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before 1992, the -- these problems with electricity were not occurring with anywhere near this kind of frequency; were they?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a lesser extent, at any rate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why is it that there was suddenly a power -- big power shortage in Banja Luka, do you know? Do you know what happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume it was because of either a total or a partial breakdown of electricity supply system throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, and as the war went on, this breakdown was getting more severe and becoming more obvious. This is all common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday, you -- during your testimony, you talked about seeing Mr. Brdjanin on TV a lot, and hearing him on the radio a lot, and you told us about some of the things that you had heard him say.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And your testimony yesterday was that that was during this period between April and December, 1992, that you heard him say these things.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both in 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But also in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Could I refer you, then, to page 20 of your statement? The paragraph that begins with, "I met Mr. Brdjanin." I think it's the second sentence in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Says, with regard to Mr. Brdjanin, "He was very frequently on the radio, TV and in the newspapers, especially in 1993. Before that, he was obviously not considered respectable as a spokesperson of the SDS. In 1991 and 1992, he was rarely interviewed." That's what you said in your statement, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With regard to his 1993 television interviews, you say in your statement that he tried to get himself on TV for discussions on regular administrative questions.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume that somebody from the television station had told you that Mr. Brdjanin was always trying to get on TV.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that someone who was close to the TV circles told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then you say that, "He tried to give the impression that he was a man of power. The way he spoke through these interviews gave the impression that he had played a very important role in Bosanska Krajina, but he never directly said that he was responsible or had given orders." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was interviews in 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes, according to the statement here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then you go on to say that, "His signature can be found on several documents about ethnic cleansing and discrimination of non-Serbs." Do you have those documents?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point, I cannot precisely refer to any document bearing his signature. However, I think that the document from Celinac concerning discrimination against non-Serb residents, which you have seen, I believe, should be consulted for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Brdjanin's name doesn't appear anywhere in that document, does it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, if you are going to ask such a direct question, I would want to have this document shown to the witness so that he is in a position to answer it, because otherwise he's going to speculate whether there is Mr. Brdjanin's name or signature on that document. He has specifically made reference to that document. Now he's being asked a very specific question, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if there's anyone in the courtroom that knows what exhibit it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- I'd appreciate being told. Otherwise I'll just plod along and find it. It will take me just a moment. It's Exhibit 450A and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's one of the documents that was introduced yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the second document, actually. The first one was 449. Mr. Krzic, please first confirm whether that -- the document that you are seeing now is the Celinac document that you referred to earlier on a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now perhaps you can answer Mr. Ackerman's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted this document to be checked for presence, if any, of Mr. Brdjanin's signature on this document. I don't have any other documents here at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you don't see a signature on that document or his name, do you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot see a signature or a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, yesterday during your testimony -- and for purposes of the Prosecution and the record, I'm referring to the LiveNote transcript at 13.11.04. That would be 13.11.04 through 13.11.17. I don't know how else to refer to it other than the time of the -- in the transcript. You said, Mr. Krzic, did you not, that -- with respect to things that you heard Mr. Brdjanin say, that he had made some very dangerous remarks to the effect that "the non-Serbian population were worms, lice, insects that had to be trodden on." That's what you told the Trial Chamber yesterday; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you personally hear Mr. Brdjanin make such statements?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if you personally heard Mr. Brdjanin make such statements, then I must ask you why you would say in your statement at the bottom of page 20: "It is known that he used such expressions," rather than, "I personally heard Mr. Brdjanin say these things."

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear similar things, such as subversive elements. I had even read such terms. I had heard him speak over the radio to the effect that Bosniaks and Croats should be prevented from doing any political work. He made similar statements for the press. And these statements were generally known and reported by numerous people in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. When it's convenient for you to stop your cross-examination for the day, please do, remembering that we still require about five minutes for Ms. Korner to deal with some organisational matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's convenient now, Your Honour. I've lost track of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think the witness can -- but we need to explain to the witness that he needs to be here again --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That has been taken care of?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He knows that. Perhaps Your Honour will be kind enough to explain something which I don't think would have arisen before. It may be in the intervening period that Mr. Krzic will meet potentially other witnesses. And if Your Honour were to explain to him that he mustn't discuss the testimony he's giving. Clearly, we can't speak to him because he's being cross-examined at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I understood yesterday from what Mr. Cayley said, that there won't be any other witnesses next week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I mean in the future, not next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. All right. Mr. Krzic, have you heard what Prosecutor Ms. Korner has just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is one of the most important principles that you have to adhere to as a witness. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand you, Your Honour, and I will adhere to that principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have not finished your evidence yet. There are some further questions that you will be asked by the Defence counsel for Mr. Brdjanin, following which there can be a re-examination from the Prosecution, possibly one or two further questions, but also this Trial Chamber may put questions to you. So it is important that between now and whenever you will be asked to come again, to return here for the next session of your evidence, you will not discuss these matters with anyone. I have your word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you may withdraw now so that we can discuss what we need to discuss. I thank you, Mr. Krzic. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, two very short matters. The first is this: We applied to Your Honours for a reconsideration of the decision in relation to protective measures, and I wonder whether Your Honours would be able to give us a decision on that, perhaps by next Wednesday. I know that people are disappearing, but clearly, we have to be in a position to deal with the potential witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that it is being taken care of. It presents more than one problem, not just the merits of it but also organisational problem. That is being considered anyway. But fortunately, between now and next Wednesday, there is ample time to go deeper into the merit and to the problem, and -- the merits of the problem and hopefully we will come down with a decision at our earliest. That's number one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, the second matter relates to your colleagues in this case. I understand that Vasiljevic has got various hearings still outstanding. I wonder whether that, for the purposes of warning our witnesses, whether that would affect our trial at all? It won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I have made sure that that won't be the case. So you can put your mind at rest. At least it's not anticipated, it's not envisaged, and precautionary measures have been taken in that regard. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the third matter is this, Your Honour: The question of hearsay evidence arose yesterday. We intend, as Your Honour knows, to deal with the question of admissibility, again, of disputed documents. I'm hoping perhaps it may be resolved this afternoon in the Status Conference, but if it isn't, we will be dealing with it. In addition to that, I wonder if I may deal with the question of hearsay, which was something that Your Honour did, in fact, make a ruling about. But it seems to me that we perhaps need a little more clarification, and I could deal with that at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, that chapter is closed and is not going to be reopened, neither the chapter on admissibility in general nor the chapter on hearsay. I don't agree with you that we have not been clear enough. We have been abundantly clear. With regard to hearsay evidence, we made it abundantly clear that that is not one of the established principles of this Tribunal. It is a characteristic that belongs more or derives more from the common law system than from other systems. This is a mixed system. And that this Tribunal, following previous decisions in regard, will adhere to what has been decided on previous occasions, that it is certainly not an absolute rule in the common law and it is certainly less absolute in this jurisdiction or in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour is absolutely right. Your Honour made it absolutely clear. All I wish to revisit is the way that Your Honour dealt with yesterday the question of some of the documentation that was submitted and how it applies, how the rule applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which documentation?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yesterday, Your Honour -- I only have the LiveNote here. When Mr. Koumjian put in documents, I think the very first two documents, from -- through Mr. Krzic, Your Honour raised the question -- in fact, this is the LiveNote version -- I'm conscious of the time. Perhaps it would be better dealt with next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It can be dealt with later but please be advised that we don't agree with you that the matter on hearsay or the position of this Trial Chamber on hearsay has not been clear enough. It has been clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position, Your Honour made absolutely clear. It is what Your Honour said yesterday that I wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I still can't place what you are referring to because the first two documents were not controversial.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was a document looking at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Reports of the -- internal reports by the party of -- by the SDA, submitted to the -- Mr. Sacirbey in New York. And the second one --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was a document that was labelled, "Personal testimony."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. That's not 449.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. It was an early document, as I say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The position was not exactly on whether it's hearsay or not. What Mr. Koumjian was trying to introduce in this -- in the records of this case was a statement made by unidentified people who preferred to remain anonymous, depriving eventually the Defence from being able to cross-examine those persons on the statements that they were making, and that statement was being presented by a witness purportedly as proving the contents thereof. It could never be accepted as a document trying to prove the contents thereof.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's just the problem, Your Honour, because that's not quite what the authority says. Of course there are degrees. But there are cases, and in the case where it's an unidentified witness, obviously, but if it's a blanket rule that Your Honour is making that it is -- that hearsay evidence can never be admitted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That specifically referred to that, directed to that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I made it clear that I would -- I wouldn't have tolerate -- I couldn't tolerate a situation whereby the witness would present that statement, say, "I had this statement made by a group of persons who described themselves at the bottom of the page as a group of," without identifying their -- themselves, and then have it presented as a document alleging this fact and that fact and that other fact, which form actually the substance of some of the charges that are being brought against the accused, and then have a situation obtain whereby Mr. Ackerman and Maitre de Roux cannot cross-examine anyone upon those facts because the authors of those -- of that document cannot be produced.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is something that is going to arise on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will deal with it as it arises, and we will deal with it in accordance with the importance of the document and whether there is a substitute for that kind of evidence or proof.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, perhaps the best thing to do, as far as we are concerned, rather than take up more time, is to see what the situation is next time it arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, also, if you are going to mention anything about this particular subject, I would suggest you don't. Okay, Mr. Ackerman, then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is two things. One is just very tangentially related to that subject, and that is, I wish we could have a rule that when Your Honours make a ruling, that that be a ruling and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need a ruling that a ruling is a ruling. A ruling is always a ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it seems like every day the Prosecutor wants to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But I have already stated that that chapter is closed. It will not be reopened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Someone needs to inform Mr. Von Heble or some of your staff that they should come collect us from the Defence room when they are ready because we are second-class citizens here, and we're not allowed access to most of this Tribunal. We just have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your client is in good company. Ms. Jarvis will deal with that. Okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am being informed, Mr. Ackerman, that you do have access to this room. It's one which is adjacent to Courtroom I, the corridor, where there is the coffee machine and the toilet. No? It's 177, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the room that's right next door to the Defence room?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. The information that I received earlier is obviously not the correct one upon cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think the Defence do have access. It's our side of the hallway --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Anyway, that will be looked into. Yesterday, Ms. Korner, we discussed very shortly with Mr. Cayley what will happen next week. Obviously, Mr. Krzic is going to be with us again, so that the cross-examination will -- of Mr. Ackerman will be terminated. Then there will be possibilities, as I said, for re-examination, if it's the case, and for some questions on our side, if it's the case, following which we discussed first whether it was wise or practical to have another witness come over. And we agreed that it's not a practical thing to do. I would invite you -- like to invite you that you try to find time in the two days we have next week to make some submissions, oral submissions, on the -- on your request to have the statement of the dead witness - I forgot his name now - be admitted into evidence. The reason is that I -- if -- perhaps you could discuss it very briefly in the presence of Mr. Von Hebel later on today. If there is agreement on the part of the Defence that there's no objection to such an admission, then you don't need to discuss. But already I have had an indication from Mr. de Roux that there is an objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will need to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour may recall that I said that Your Honours might feel that it was better left until we've heard in fact the last witness, because he's going to be dealing with the military --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm perfectly prepared to argue it on the merits without that, but the relevance or otherwise will become apparent when that witness testifies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I'm prepared to do it next week if Your Honour wants me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The important thing is that if we eventually have to come to that, that it will not stop us from -- in other words, at least if we have the submissions, then if we have to cross that juncture, we will be prepared for it and we would be able to do it straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm perfectly prepared if there's time next week, which there probably will be, to deal with the matter then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. If you could find time, I think that would be useful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay? Thank you. So we will continue on the 13th. That's Wednesday, Wednesday. That's Wednesday. And we will continue with the cross-examination or what's left of the cross-examination of -- yes, at 9.00 -- the cross-examination of Mr. Krzic. I thank you.
